entries: Field sampling and measurement | Plan and sites | Take part in geological, geophysical, geochemical, or marine surveys, reconnaissance, drilling, and logging projects according to the plan, install and operate instruments, collect solid or fluid samples, and measure field parameters.

Sample preparation, testing, and data | Instruments and records | Use laboratory instruments or testing equipment to prepare and test samples to determine composition and characteristics, and compile, record, and enter testing or operating data for review and further analysis.

Charts and report outputs | Sketches, cross sections, and reports | Prepare notes, sketches, and geological maps or cross sections, record characteristics such as the pressure and temperature of wells or bore holes, and prepare or review technical reports on sampling, testing, and data analysis.

Equipment and field maintenance | Operation and calibration | Operate and adjust the equipment and instruments used to obtain geological data, maintain field equipment, install and recover sampling equipment, and handle samples and send them to the testing laboratory.

Quality and safety control | Blanks, replicates, and boundaries | Use field blanks, replicate samples, and calibration records according to the plan to control quality and validate data, and confirm the boundaries of environment, energy, and personnel safety according to project procedures.

Collaboration and handover | Chain and traceability | Communicate with scientists, engineers, and the team and advance according to the plan, and complete the chain-of-custody handover of samples, data, and records while keeping them traceable.

paragraphs: Adjacent occupations are compared by main object and output, and sampling, analysis, QC, and reporting often overlap. This occupation supports resource, well bore, and laboratory data; geodetic surveying focuses on control coordinates, mining and petroleum engineering on design schemes, environmental science on monitoring and assessment, and hydrologists on hydrologic processes and water resource problems. The title does not grant or exclude signing or acceptance authority.

Evidence note | The comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupation classification and public materials, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and to support fit choices; they do not constitute qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions, nor do they constitute engineering, geological, environmental, or safety advice. The wages and employment of each occupation must be checked separately against its own SOC measure; this table does not compare values or treat one occupation's wages as a proxy for another; field safety and data and environmental requirements must be checked against each jurisdiction and institution. The U.S. wages and employment on this page use this occupation's own 19-4043.00 measure, using only the official values of this occupation (19-4043.00) itself.

Preface | The comparison below is organized in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key difference — what it is better suited to'. Sampling, testing, measurement, engineering design, and environmental assessment are often linked within the same project or institution, but linkage does not mean they are interchangeable; when choosing across directions, the methods, specifications, authorization, and responsibility boundaries of that direction must be learned anew.

Tasks overlap: environmental scientists may sample, analyze, and perform QC, engineers may review records and equipment, and geological technicians may take part in water-related surveys. Adjacent positions cannot be described as not carrying quality or safety responsibility, and modeling cannot be prohibited by name; the specific division of work, methods, and responsibility are checked per project.

Better suited to people who are willing to move between the laboratory, well bores, and exploration sites, can strictly follow numbering, calibration, and recording rules, and retest and report when anomalies are found.

Core work and outputs: take part in geological, geophysical, geochemical, or marine surveys, reconnaissance, drilling, and logging projects according to the plan and collect solid or fluid samples; use laboratory instruments or testing equipment to prepare and test samples and compile, record, and enter data; record characteristics such as the pressure and temperature of wells or bore holes and maintain field equipment and install and recover sampling equipment; prepare notes, sketches, and geological maps or cross sections and record characteristics such as the pressure and temperature of wells or bore holes; prepare or review technical reports on sampling, testing, and data analysis; outputs are samples and testing data and field records and charts and reports (O*NET/SOC 19-4043.00, Geological Technicians, Except Hydrologic Technicians).
This occupation: Geological Technicians, Except Hydrologic Technicians (O*NET/SOC 19-4043.00 Geological Technicians, Except Hydrologic Technicians)

Key difference: geodetic surveyors take control network layout, observation, computation, and delivery of results as their object, and produce survey control results and coordinate and elevation data; this occupation takes samples, testing, and field data as its object and usually does not carry responsibility for control surveying or issuing survey results (but must collaborate with it and share the position datum).

Better suited to people who want to work on control surveying, instrument observation, computation, and delivery of results; this occupation leans more toward samples, testing, field data, and equipment maintenance.

Core work and outputs: lay out and observe control networks and process observation data, compute coordinates and elevations and prepare survey results and notes, and support engineering, cadastral, and resource surveys; outputs are survey control results, coordinate and elevation data, and survey reports.
Geodetic Surveyors (17-1022.01)

Key difference: mining and geological engineers take scheme design, resource evaluation, and engineering design as their object, and produce design schemes and professional conclusions; this occupation carries out sampling, testing, and recording according to the plan and does not carry responsibility for engineering design or reserve evaluation (but must provide data and sample support for them). Signing or acceptance authority is checked against the actual appointment, jurisdiction, and qualifications and is not granted by the occupational description itself.

Willingness to explore engineering design, resource evaluation, calculation, and professional judgment directions; check the target training and actual duties, and signing/acceptance authority is checked separately against jurisdiction, qualifications, and appointment.

Design extraction or exploration schemes, carry out resource evaluation and engineering calculations, assess geological conditions and risks, and prepare designs and reports. Signing/acceptance authority is checked against actual qualifications, jurisdiction, and appointment and is not automatically granted by the occupation name.
Mining and Geological Engineers (17-2151.00)

Key difference: petroleum engineers take drilling, completion, and production scheme design and optimization as their object, and produce engineering schemes and professional conclusions; this occupation carries out sample collection, testing, and recording according to the plan and usually does not carry responsibility for oil and gas engineering design or operational decisions. Signing or acceptance authority is checked against the actual appointment, jurisdiction, and qualifications and is not granted by the occupational description itself.

Better suited to people who want to work on oil and gas engineering scheme design, calculation, and optimization; this occupation leans more toward field sampling, testing, data, and equipment maintenance.

Core work and outputs: design drilling, completion, production, and stimulation schemes and carry out calculations and economic evaluations, assess operating risks, and prepare schemes and reports; outputs are engineering schemes and professional conclusions.
Petroleum Engineers (17-2171.00)

Key difference: environmental scientists and specialists take research and assessment of environmental monitoring, pollution, ecological, and resource problems as their object, and produce assessment reports and protection recommendations; this occupation takes sampling, testing, and field data as its object and usually does not carry responsibility for environmental compliance assessment or enforcement-related conclusions (but must provide data support for them).

Better suited to people who want to work on environmental monitoring, experimentation, assessment, and protection recommendations; this occupation leans more toward field sampling, testing, equipment, and data recording.

Core work and outputs: design and carry out environmental sampling, monitoring, and experimentation, analyze pollution, ecological, and resource problems and assess impacts, prepare assessment reports and protection recommendations, and take part in policy and public communication; outputs are monitoring and assessment reports and recommendations.
Environmental Scientists and Specialists (19-2041.00)

Hydrologists focus on hydrologic processes, models, water resources, and flood problems; geological technicians focus on resource, well bore, and laboratory data and may also take part in hydrologic surveys and groundwater collaboration. subject.name: Geological Technicians, Except Hydrologic Technicians
subject.summary: This page corresponds to O*NET19-4043.00 geological technicians (excluding hydrologic technicians), who assist scientists or engineers in obtaining resource, well bore, and laboratory data, collect and prepare solid or fluid samples, analyze mud and drill cuttings, record characteristics such as pressure and temperature, and chart and report. It excludes independent hydrologic technicians 19-4044 and the petroleum pump station operation occupation, but this does not mean all water-related tasks are prohibited: the tasks of this occupation may include hydrologic surveys and groundwater monitoring collaboration.
